title: OmniNav: Unified Framework for Embodied Navigation
one_liner: A robot can navigate using a single model that handles spoken instructions, object targets, goal points, and self-directed exploration by using a fast brain for quick moves and a slow brain for long-term planning.
lead: When a robot needs to navigate, it might be told go to the kitchen, or find a coffee mug, or explore the room. Today's models handle only one of these at a time, and they trip over real walls and cluttered spaces. OmniNav solves this by building one navigation engine that handles all four tasks in a single brain, using fast reflexes for moment-to-moment movement and slow deliberation for longer paths.

paras: A robot moving through a real room has four different jobs: follow a spoken instruction like go to the kitchen, search for an object like find the coffee mug, move to a specific point on a map, or explore unknown territory on its own. Today's best models handle one job well, but fall apart at the others.

A naive approach is to build four separate models, one per task. But that is wasteful and brittle. When the robot encounters something unexpected — a hallway that looks like the kitchen, a mug-shaped shadow, a path that shifts — each model fails differently, and the robot has no unified way to reason across tasks. A beginner might try to bolt them together with switching logic, but then every decision point becomes a brittle rule that does not transfer to new buildings or lighting.

callout.html: OmniNav trains one navigation model that handles spoken directions, object search, point goals, and autonomous exploration all at once, using a split brain: fast reflexes for immediate steps, slow planning for long routes.

steps.text: Camera image plus either a spoken instruction, object name, goal location, or exploration flag.
Looks at the last few frames and generates a waypoint — a concrete coordinate and rotation for the next 0.2 seconds.
Every 2 seconds, examines a longer history, estimates which frontiers (unexplored edges) are best to visit next, and recommends a new subgoal.
The fast module biases its waypoints toward the slow module's recommendation without getting locked in.
Executes the waypoint at 5 Hz (five times per second), feeding new images back into the cycle.

paras: The paper moves from four separate navigation policies to a single unified policy. The key change: instead of outputting discrete actions like forward, left, or right, the policy predicts continuous waypoints — actual coordinates where the robot should move and how it should rotate.

hidden.name: Frontier importance score
paras: A frontier is the edge between explored and unexplored territory — the boundary of what the robot has seen so far. Every frontier looks different: some are short hallways, some are glass walls the camera cannot see through, some are openings to large spaces. The paper measures each frontier's importance — which frontiers are worth visiting based on the current task and the robot's position.

The slow module estimates importance by looking at the visual features around each frontier boundary, learned from training on exploration and navigation datasets. High importance means visit this frontier; low importance means it is probably already explored or leads nowhere useful. This hidden quantity is what makes the split brain work: the fast reflexes do not have to predict the entire path, because the slow planner communicates importance to steer them.

heat.caption: Darker frontiers are worth exploring; lighter ones are bypassed because they lead to dead ends or already-visited territory.

reads.html: The slow module watches which parts of the unseen boundary are most promising right now, using clues from the visual scene.
Long-horizon observations and candidate frontier features are scored by the slow module to select the next subgoal and subtask.

paras: The core problem is that four different tasks demand very different planning horizons. Following a spoken instruction like go to the kitchen requires understanding the whole room layout, which takes seconds of observation. But the robot needs to move every 0.2 seconds or it stops. A single model trying to handle both would either be too slow (deliberating 2 seconds before each move) or too myopic (never thinking past the next corner).

OmniNav solves this by splitting into two processes: the fast module watches only the last few frames and outputs a concrete next step every 0.2 seconds. This keeps the robot responsive. The slow module, running every 2 seconds, examines a much longer history and decides what the overall goal should be — which frontier to head toward, whether to stick with the current task or switch, how to interpret the instruction in this specific room. The fast module does not ignore the slow module; instead, it biases its waypoints toward wherever the slow module says to go, but stays ready to dodge obstacles the slow module did not see.

This works because real navigation is hierarchical: every detailed movement contributes to a larger plan, and every large plan is composed of many small movements. By running both timescales at once, the model stays responsive and also stays on track.

math.words: The waypoint prediction combines the fast module's immediate sensory read with a weighted bias toward the slow module's frontier recommendation. The loss penalizes distance between predicted waypoint and ground truth, with higher penalty for navigation tasks that require long-term coherence.
math.equation: L_total = L_waypoint_fast + alpha * L_alignment + beta * L_frontier_matching
symbols: error between predicted waypoint and actual next move
penalty for disagreeing with the slow module's direction
penalty for not moving toward recommended frontiers
weight balancing fast and slow modules (learned during training)
weight emphasizing frontier coherence (learned during training)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the robot is exploring and needs to visit frontier 3. Fast module predicts waypoint at heading 45 degrees. Slow module recommends heading 40 degrees toward frontier 3.
L_alignment = (45 - 40)^2 = 25 degrees squared (fast and slow disagree a little).
L_frontier_matching = measure of how much the path moves toward frontier 3 = 8 units.
Training updates weights to lower L_total, pulling fast and slow into agreement and steering toward the frontier.

math.note: The fast module learns to predict accurate immediate moves; the slow module learns to pick good frontiers; the alignment term makes them cooperate.

charts.title: Four separate models
charts.note: Each excels at one task but fails badly at others; no unified solution.

charts.title: OmniNav unified model
charts.note: Single model handles all tasks with consistent, high performance. The slow planner lifts exploration performance from 65% to 82%.

items.html: If the spoken instruction is ambiguous or describes a room layout that does not match reality, the slow module misestimates what the goal actually is. The robot ends up in the wrong kitchen. The paper notes that this is the bottleneck — instruction understanding, not path planning — so they added extra training data from image captioning and referring/grounding datasets.

The slow module might rate a frontier as highly important because it looks like the target object, but the frontier is actually a mirror or a reflective surface. The robot pushes toward an impossible target. Real-world testing catches this, but sim-only training is vulnerable.

If the fast and slow modules are too misaligned, they fight each other — fast module tries to dodge left, slow module pulls right, and the robot stutters. Training with the alignment loss prevents this, but if the weights are too aggressive, fast becomes just a slave to slow.

Train on mixed tasks (instructions, objects, points, exploration), use general-purpose image understanding datasets to ground instruction and object language, balance the fast-slow collaboration with realistic weights, and test on real robots. The paper does this, scoring higher than other methods on standard benchmarks and validating on real hardware.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal sim with a simple square room, a few objects, and a robot with a camera. Train or load a pretrained OmniNav model. Run four trials to test each navigation mode that the paper claims to solve: (1) give a spoken goal like go to the red block, (2) say find the mug, (3) provide GPS coordinates to a target point, (4) enable exploration mode and let it wander. Measure success as reaching the goal or covering the unexplored area, because the paper's central claim is handling all four modes in one model. Each trial fails if the robot cannot complete the task within 300 steps or five minutes of simulated time.
demo.metric_eq: Success rate per task = (trials reaching goal or target) / (total trials per task). Unified model should achieve >75% on all four; separate models should have >80% on their own task but <60% on others.
demo.closing: If you run the demo with fast-slow disabled (just the fast module predicting raw waypoints), the robot meanders in all four tasks because it has no long-term plan. If slow is disabled, the robot becomes reactive and never looks far enough ahead. With both running together, the robot solves all four at once because the split timescales align speed with planning depth.
